title: A fully discrete LBRFD-IPDG method for linear fourth-order parabolic equations
summary: We propose a fully discrete method for linear fourth-order parabolic equations with Dirichlet boundary conditions, combining an implicit LBRFD multistep scheme in time with a mixed interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin (IPDG) method in space. The temporal discretization employs equispaced linear barycentric rational interpolants and incorporates a startup procedure. To facilitate the spatial discretization, the original problem is reformulated through an auxiliary variable. For certain parameter pairs $(n,d)$, the LBRFD method is shown to be $A(α)$-stable and to possess a wider stability angle than the corresponding BDF$p$ method of the same order. Stability and a priori error estimates are established via a $G$-energy technique and the discrete Grönwall lemma. The theoretical analysis yields a total $L^2$ error estimate of order $h^{k-1}+τ^p$, where $p=d$ if $n-d$ is even and $p=d+1$ if $n-d$ is odd. The reduced spatial convergence rate is attributed to boundary contributions on $\partialΩ$. Despite this theoretical prediction, numerical experiments confirm the stability and demonstrate optimal convergence of order $h^{k+1}+τ^p$.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a fully discrete method combining an implicit linear barycentric rational finite difference (LBRFD) multistep scheme in time with a mixed interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin (IPDG) method in space for linear fourth-order parabolic equations with Dirichlet boundary conditions. The method achieves A(α)-stability for certain parameter pairs, and theoretical error analysis yields O(h^{k-1}+τ^p), while numerical experiments demonstrate optimal convergence of order h^{k+1}+τ^p.
AI.motivation: To develop a stable and accurate fully discrete numerical method for fourth-order parabolic equations with Dirichlet boundary conditions, addressing challenges in both temporal and spatial discretization while achieving desirable stability properties comparable to or better than standard multistep methods.
AI.method: Combines an implicit LBRFD multistep scheme for temporal discretization (using equispaced linear barycentric rational interpolants with a startup procedure) with a mixed IPDG method in space (reformulating the problem through an auxiliary variable). Stability and error estimates are established using a G-energy technique and the discrete Grönwall lemma.
AI.result: The LBRFD method is shown to be A(α)-stable with a wider stability angle than BDFp of the same order for certain (n,d) parameter pairs. Theoretical analysis gives a total L² error of order h^{k-1}+τ^p (where p=d for even n-d and p=d+1 for odd n-d), with the reduced spatial convergence attributed to boundary contributions. Numerical experiments confirm stability and show optimal convergence of order h^{k+1}+τ^p.
AI.conclusion: The proposed fully discrete method is stable and effective for linear fourth-order parabolic equations. While theoretical analysis predicts a suboptimal spatial convergence rate due to boundary effects, numerical results demonstrate optimal convergence, suggesting the theoretical bound may be improvable or the boundary contributions are not significant in practice.

title: A High-Order Rank-Adaptive Implicit Algorithm for Solving High Dimensional Diffusion Equations using the Hierarchical Tucker Decomposition
comment: This work was done while PBP was an undergraduate at Swarthmore College. Project Advisor: Dr. Joseph Nakao (Swarthmore College)
summary: This paper presents a high-order rank-adaptive implicit integrator for the tensor solution of high-dimensional diffusion equations. We extend the 3D version of this method from the Tucker decomposition to higher dimensions using the hierarchical Tucker (HT) decomposition, since the storage complexity for the Tucker decomposition increases exponentially with the number of dimensions $d>3$. The HT format avoids this issue by decomposing the solution according to a binary tree consisting of bases for each dimension and core tensors which connect the bases. Spectral methods are considered for spatial discretization, and diagonally implicit Runge-Kutta methods are considered for time discretization. At each stage of the Runge-Kutta method, the bases computed at the previous stages are augmented to predict the upcoming basis and construct projection subspaces. By projecting onto these enriched subspaces, the bases and cores can be updated in a sequential manner going up the tree from leaf-to-root. Unlike the 3D Tucker method which has a single core tensor, the HT method also updates the intermediate core tensors. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the method observes high-order accuracy, and test how well the integrator captures the solution rank for various sets of time-dependent diffusion coefficients.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a high-order rank-adaptive implicit integrator for solving high-dimensional diffusion equations using the hierarchical Tucker (HT) decomposition, extending a prior 3D Tucker-based method. The HT format avoids the exponential storage cost of Tucker for d>3 by decomposing solutions along a binary tree with per-dimension bases and connecting core tensors. The method uses spectral spatial discretization and diagonally implicit Runge-Kutta methods, updating bases and cores leaf-to-root via enriched projection subspaces. Numerical experiments demonstrate high-order accuracy and rank-capturing behavior.
AI.motivation: The Tucker decomposition used in the existing 3D method suffers from exponential storage complexity when extended to higher dimensions (d>3), motivating the need for a more scalable tensor format like hierarchical Tucker (HT) for high-dimensional diffusion equations.
AI.method: The method combines HT tensor decomposition with diagonally implicit Runge-Kutta time integrators and spectral spatial discretization. At each RK stage, previously computed bases are augmented to predict upcoming bases and build projection subspaces; projecting onto these enriched subspaces enables sequential leaf-to-root updates of bases and core tensors, including intermediate core tensors not present in the 3D Tucker approach.
AI.result: Numerical experiments show the integrator achieves high-order accuracy and effectively captures the solution rank for various time-dependent diffusion coefficient scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The HT-based rank-adaptive implicit integrator successfully generalizes the 3D Tucker method to arbitrary dimensions while overcoming the exponential storage limitation, offering a scalable approach for high-dimensional diffusion equation solving.

title: A high-order, meshless, Lagrangian--Eulerian RBF-FD method for advection--diffusion--reaction on moving manifolds
summary: We present a high-order radial basis function-generated finite difference (RBF-FD) method for partial differential equations on moving manifolds $\mathcal M(t)\subset\mathbb R^3$ of co-dimension one. Our method builds on the tangent-plane formulation of surface RBF-FD and combines Lagrangian and Eulerian treatments: the manifold and material derivative are evolved in a Lagrangian fashion, while the remaining surface differential operators are reconstructed on the instantaneous point cloud and stabilized, when necessary, by a quasi-analytical hyperviscosity formulation. Lagrangian marker drift is handled by adaptive rearrangement using a compact global parametric model of the moving surface, which also supplies accurate normals and geometry-based quadrature. After rearrangement, we reconstruct the multistep history by backward semi-Lagrangian tracing and interpolation before resuming the Lagrangian time discretization. We exploit temporal coherence through three update strategies: defect correction for the local RBF-FD weights, a curvature-based update of the hyperviscosity coefficients between spectral recomputations, and a global defect-correction iteration that reuses an incomplete LU (ILU) factorization before preconditioned generalized minimal residual (GMRES) iterations. Finally, we enforce the prescribed global mass balance through a scalar projection based on the evolving surface quadrature. Numerical experiments demonstrate high-order convergence, conservation to roundoff in source-free problems, stable long-time integration, and substantial savings from the proposed update strategies.

AI.tldr: A high-order RBF-FD method for PDEs on moving co-dimension one manifolds in R^3, combining Lagrangian/Eulerian treatments with adaptive rearrangement, semi-Lagrangian reconstruction, temporal coherence strategies, and mass-conservation projection.
AI.motivation: To develop an accurate and efficient numerical method for solving partial differential equations on moving surfaces embedded in 3D, where Lagrangian marker drift and computational cost are key challenges.
AI.method: Builds on tangent-plane surface RBF-FD; evolves manifold and material derivative in Lagrangian fashion while reconstructing surface differential operators on instantaneous point clouds; uses quasi-analytical hyperviscosity stabilization; handles marker drift via adaptive rearrangement with a compact global parametric model; reconstructs multistep history by backward semi-Lagrangian tracing; employs defect correction for RBF-FD weights, curvature-based hyperviscosity updates, and ILU-reused GMRES; enforces mass balance via scalar projection.
AI.result: Numerical experiments show high-order convergence, conservation to roundoff in source-free problems, stable long-time integration, and substantial computational savings from the proposed update strategies.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method achieves high-order accuracy and robust conservation for PDEs on moving manifolds with significant computational efficiency gains.

title: Implicit-adjoint finite-volume topology optimization of two-dimensional conjugate heat transfer
summary:
Designing compact, high-efficiency thermal architectures requires resolving the competing demands of solid conduction, fluid convection, and flow resistance within highly constrained physical envelopes. Density-based topology optimization provides a systematic framework for synthesizing these coupled layouts, yet the reproducibility and numerical stability of the resulting designs depend critically on the underlying discrete solvers and adjoint sensitivity mechanics. In this work, we present a transparent, self-contained two-dimensional finite-volume formulation on a staggered Marker-and-Cell grid for conjugate heat transfer governed by design-dependent energy transport coupled to Stokes--Brinkman or Darcy flow at fixed solid volume. To prevent spurious artificial thermal sources in porous, weakly compressible Brinkman domains, the discrete advection operator is constructed to satisfy the identity $\mathbf{u}\cdot
abla T=
abla\cdot(\mathbf{u}T)-T(
abla\cdot\mathbf{u})$ cellwise, ensuring that uniform temperature fields remain exact discrete nullspaces even under inexact continuity satisfaction. Reverse-mode derivatives are evaluated via the implicit function theorem rather than unrolled iterative loops, yielding exact discrete adjoints with bounded memory requirements. The discrete operators are systematically validated through the method of manufactured solutions and directional Taylor remainder tests. Four representative thermofluid design benchmarks are optimized using a projected-gradient scheme with $β$-continuation, wherein candidate iterates are accepted and published only upon satisfying rigorous, predeclared gates on residual convergence, mass conservation, volume feasibility, and numerical finiteness. The resulting formulation provides an inspectable, deterministic reference stack for verifiable conjugate thermofluidic topology optimization.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a transparent, self-contained 2D finite-volume formulation on a staggered Marker-and-Cell grid for conjugate heat transfer topology optimization, coupled with Stokes-Brinkman or Darcy flow. It introduces a discrete advection operator that ensures uniform temperature fields remain exact nullspaces, uses implicit function theorem for exact discrete adjoints with bounded memory, and validates all discrete operators via manufactured solutions and Taylor remainder tests. Four thermofluid design benchmarks are optimized with strict convergence gates for reproducible, verifiable results.
AI.motivation: Density-based topology optimization for thermal-fluid systems requires resolving competing demands of conduction, convection, and flow resistance, but reproducibility and numerical stability depend critically on the underlying discrete solvers and adjoint sensitivity mechanics, which are often opaque or unstable.
AI.method: A 2D finite-volume formulation on a staggered Marker-and-Cell grid is developed for conjugate heat transfer with design-dependent energy transport coupled to Stokes-Brinkman or Darcy flow. The discrete advection operator satisfies the identity u·∇T=∇·(uT)-T(∇·u) cellwise to prevent spurious thermal sources. Reverse-mode derivatives use the implicit function theorem for exact discrete adjoints. Validation uses manufactured solutions and directional Taylor remainder tests, with a projected-gradient scheme and β-continuation under strict convergence gates.
AI.result: The discrete operators pass method-of-manufactured-solutions and Taylor remainder validation. Four representative thermofluid design benchmarks are successfully optimized with iterates accepted only upon satisfying predeclared gates on residual convergence, mass conservation, volume feasibility, and numerical finiteness, yielding reproducible designs.
AI.conclusion: The formulation provides an inspectable, deterministic reference stack for verifiable conjugate thermofluidic topology optimization, addressing reproducibility and numerical stability challenges in the field.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks as Fast Surrogate Models for Electrochemical Flow Reactors
summary: This work presents a physics-informed neural network (PINN) for modeling a transient two-dimensional electrochemical flow reactor with diffusion, migration, convection, and nonlinear anodic Butler--Volmer kinetics. The model is trained without labeled concentration data by embedding the governing transport equation and all initial and boundary conditions into a composite loss function. Spatial and temporal coordinates together with anodic overpotential, temperature, inlet concentration, maximum flow velocity, and diffusivity are used as inputs, allowing the network to predict concentration fields over a broad operating domain. Validation against finite-difference-based solutions shows strong agreement for representative transient and near-steady cases, with a mean relative space--time error of $(9.99 \pm 0.65)\times10^{-3}$ (sub-percent level) across the conditioning domain. PINN inference is faster than a traditional finite difference solver by a factor of $5.34$, thus reducing runtime by $81.3\%$. Generalization tests further show that the surrogate remains robust under in-domain boundary-focused sampling and controlled extrapolation, although anodic overpotential is the most challenging parameter due to its exponential effect on interfacial kinetics. The results indicate that physics-informed neural networks can serve as accurate and efficient parametric surrogates for electrochemical transport problems and provide a foundation for low-computational-cost digital-twin modeling of electrochemical flow reactors.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a physics-informed neural network (PINN) for modeling a transient 2D electrochemical flow reactor with diffusion, migration, convection, and nonlinear Butler-Volmer kinetics. The model is trained without labeled data by embedding governing equations and boundary conditions into a composite loss function, achieving sub-percent accuracy (mean relative error ~1%), running 5.34× faster than finite-difference solvers, and showing robustness under in-domain sampling and controlled extrapolation.
AI.motivation: Traditional numerical solvers for electrochemical flow reactors (e.g., finite-difference methods) are computationally expensive, limiting their use in real-time digital-twin applications. A fast and accurate parametric surrogate is needed.
AI.method: A PINN is trained with a composite physics-based loss function (governing transport equations + initial/boundary conditions) without labeled concentration data. Inputs include spatial/temporal coordinates plus operating parameters (anodic overpotential, temperature, inlet concentration, max flow velocity, diffusivity). The network predicts concentration fields across a broad operating domain.
AI.result: Validation against finite-difference solutions shows strong agreement with mean relative space-time error of (9.99±0.65)×10⁻³ (sub-percent). PINN inference is 5.34× faster than the finite-difference solver (81.3% runtime reduction). Generalization tests confirm robustness under in-domain boundary-focused sampling and controlled extrapolation, with anodic overpotential being the most challenging parameter due to its exponential effect on kinetics.
AI.conclusion: Physics-informed neural networks can serve as accurate and efficient parametric surrogates for electrochemical transport problems, providing a foundation for low-computational-cost digital-twin modeling of electrochemical flow reactors.

title: Real-time feedback control of ELM frequency using divertor gas puffing and its effects on tungsten-induced radiation and plasma performance in KSTAR
summary: The edge-localized mode (ELM) frequency ($f_{\mathrm{ELM}}$) was successfully controlled in real time on KSTAR using a proportional-integral (PI) feedback controller, employing a $\mathrm{D}_2$ divertor gas puff as the actuator under tungsten lower-divertor conditions. The controller accurately tracked a two-step target---a 30 Hz increase in $f_{\mathrm{ELM}}$ for 4 s, followed by a 30 Hz decrease for 3 s---yielding mean and median absolute percentage errors of approximately 13% and 12%, respectively. Compared to a reference discharge, the actively controlled shot did not exhibit a significant drop in volume-integrated core radiation, confirming that excessive gas use merely degrades overall plasma performance. However, when contrasted with the exponential increase in core radiation observed in the absence of divertor gas puffing, these results underscore the critical need for real-time optimization. Specifically, divertor gas commands must be actively managed to maintain an $f_{\mathrm{ELM}}$ sufficient for flushing tungsten from the core while maximizing global plasma performance.

AI.tldr: Real-time PI feedback control of ELM frequency using D2 divertor gas puffing was demonstrated on KSTAR, achieving ~13% mean absolute error tracking a two-step frequency target while preserving core plasma performance.
AI.motivation: To avoid excessive gas use that degrades plasma performance, there is a need for real-time optimization of divertor gas commands to maintain sufficient ELM frequency for tungsten flushing while maximizing global plasma performance.
AI.method: A proportional-integral (PI) feedback controller was implemented on KSTAR to control ELM frequency in real time, using a D2 divertor gas puff as the actuator under tungsten lower-divertor conditions.
AI.result: The controller tracked a two-step target (30 Hz increase for 4s, then 30 Hz decrease for 3s) with mean and median absolute percentage errors of ~13% and ~12%. No significant drop in volume-integrated core radiation was observed compared to a reference discharge.
AI.conclusion: Real-time control of ELM frequency via divertor gas puffing is feasible while preserving performance, and active management is critical to balance tungsten flushing and global plasma performance.

title: The Liquid Drop Model with a Yukawa Potential: Existence of Minimizers and Sharp Stability of the Ball
summary: We study a long-range perturbation of the perimeter functional by a nonlocal repulsive term defined through the Yukawa kernel, minimized under a volume constraint. Because the kernel decays exponentially, the competition between surface tension and repulsion is governed by two independent quantities, the screening rate and the volume. Specifically we prove that (i) above an explicit critical screening rate, minimizers exist at every volume, whereas earlier work required the volume to be large; (ii) below an explicit volume threshold minimizers exist for every screening rate; (iii) at small volume, and uniformly in the screening rate, the ball is the unique minimizer up to translation; and (iv) there exists a sharp volume threshold, depending on the screening rate, for the ball to be a stable volume-constrained critical point. The threshold is given in closed form for every screening rate and reduces to the known unscreened value when $α=0$. Our proofs overcome new technical changes due to the lack of homogeneity in the Yukawa kernel.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the minimization of a perimeter functional perturbed by a long-range nonlocal repulsive term with the Yukawa kernel under a volume constraint. It proves existence theorems, uniqueness of the ball at small volume, and a sharp stability threshold for the ball, overcoming challenges due to the kernel's lack of homogeneity.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to extend prior results on nonlocal perimeter minimization by establishing minimizer existence under broader conditions (no longer requiring large volume), and to characterize when the ball is the unique minimizer or a stable critical point. The Yukawa kernel's exponential decay introduces a screening parameter, making the analysis novel and more physically relevant.
AI.method: The authors analyze a competition between surface tension and nonlocal repulsion governed by the screening rate and volume. They prove existence via critical screening rates and volume thresholds, establish uniqueness of the ball at small volume uniformly in the screening rate, and derive a sharp volume threshold for stability of the ball as a constrained critical point, all while handling the non-homogeneous nature of the Yukawa kernel.
AI.result: (i) Above an explicit critical screening rate, minimizers exist at every volume. (ii) Below an explicit volume threshold, minimizers exist for every screening rate. (iii) At small volume, the ball is the unique minimizer up to translation, uniformly in the screening rate. (iv) A sharp volume threshold for the ball to be a stable volume-constrained critical point is provided in closed form, reducing to the known unscreened value when α=0.
AI.conclusion: The paper fully characterizes existence and stability of minimizers for the Yukawa perturbed perimeter functional, providing explicit thresholds in both screening rate and volume. The results generalize previous unscreened findings and overcome technical difficulties from the kernel's lack of homogeneity.

title: The Normal Procrustes Problem: A Riemannian Optimization Approach
comment: 41 pages, 10 figures. Code available at https://github.com/kbierly/NPP
summary: For given $m \times n$ data matrices $X, Y$, we investigate the Normal Procrustes Problem---the least squares optimization problem that aims to minimize $\|AX-Y\|_F^2$, where $A$ is constrained to be a normal $m \times m$ matrix. As far as the author of this article is aware, no other method that attempts to solve the Normal Procrustes Problem exists in the literature; we thus propose what is, to our knowledge, the first such method. We, furthermore, adapt our approach to address the Real Normal Procrustes Problem, where $A$ must be real. In our treatment of these problems, we first reduce our complex and real objective functions to be purely optimizable over the Riemannian manifolds of the unitary and real orthogonal matrices, respectively. This reduction enables us to apply techniques in Riemannian manifold optimization to approximate solutions to both. The Closest Normal Matrix and Real Closest Normal Matrix Problems are both special cases of their respective Procrustes Problems and have been previously studied in the literature. Our approach thus recovers a novel Riemannian optimization method for approximating solutions to both these problems. We further numerically test the performance of our method across all such problems (including against previously developed algorithms on the Closest Normal Matrix Problems) and obtain competitive residuals and favorable scaling in wall-clock time.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the first method to solve the Normal Procrustes Problem (minimizing ||AX-Y||_F² with A normal) and its real variant, by reducing the optimization to Riemannian manifolds of unitary and real orthogonal matrices, then applying Riemannian manifold optimization techniques. The method also recovers a novel approach for the special-case Closest Normal Matrix Problems.
AI.motivation: The Normal Procrustes Problem has not been addressed in the literature despite being a natural extension of the classical Procrustes Problem. The authors aim to fill this gap by proposing the first solution method, while also improving upon existing approaches to the closely related Closest Normal Matrix Problems.
AI.method: The authors reduce the complex and real objective functions of the Normal Procrustes Problems to be optimizable over Riemannian manifolds of unitary matrices (complex case) and real orthogonal matrices (real case). They then apply Riemannian manifold optimization techniques to approximate solutions to both problems.
AI.result: Numerical experiments across all problems (including comparisons against previously developed algorithms on the Closest Normal Matrix Problems) demonstrate competitive residuals and favorable scaling in wall-clock time.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Riemannian optimization approach provides an effective and scalable first solution to the Normal Procrustes Problem, and also improves upon existing methods for the Closest Normal Matrix Problems as special cases.

title: Diagonalization of the Landau Hamiltonian with a Periodic Potential via a Galerkin Projection Method and Applications to Topological Band Properties
summary: In this paper, we study the numerical computation of eigenfunctions of the Landau Hamiltonian with a periodic potential. We propose a spectral method using the eigenfunctions of the Landau operator that allows us to numerically compute the band structure for potentials of different strengths, including the well-studied weak and strong potentials, and additionally systems in the intermediate regime. We then apply the method to simulations across the full range of coupling constants from weak to strong coupling and present an analysis of the band structure as a function of the potential strength.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a spectral method for numerically computing eigenfunctions and band structures of the Landau Hamiltonian with a periodic potential, covering weak to strong coupling regimes.
AI.motivation: To numerically compute eigenfunctions of the Landau Hamiltonian with a periodic potential across all coupling regimes, including the intermediate regime that has been less studied compared to the well-understood weak and strong potential limits.
AI.method: A spectral method that uses the eigenfunctions of the Landau operator as a basis to compute the band structure for periodic potentials of varying strengths.
AI.result: The method successfully computes band structures across the full range of coupling constants, from weak to strong coupling, enabling analysis of the band structure as a function of potential strength.
AI.conclusion: The proposed spectral method bridges the gap between weak and strong potential regimes, providing a unified numerical framework and insights into how the band structure evolves with potential strength.

title: Informing spectral models for dense plasmas with K-edge absorption measurements of warm dense copper
summary: Warm dense matter remains a challenging regime to characterize experimentally and to model with predictive accuracy. Recent experimental platforms have been developed to generate, characterize, and diagnose uniform warm dense matter, enabling detailed comparisons with models. Here, we present experiments conducted at the OMEGA laser facility that compress and heat a buried layer target to warm dense matter conditions, where the targets are heated to temperatures of approximately 20 eV and compressed to densities of 25 g/cm^3. We probe the warm dense plasma using x-ray absorption spectroscopy, using the K-edge and bound-bound absorption features to constrain the temperature and charge state distribution of the plasma. We compare these measurements with two types of models: collisional-radiative models with detailed electronic structure and ad-hoc density effects, and a multi-ion model based on density functional theory in combination with excited-state projector augmented-wave potentials. Neither approach fully reproduces the observed data, We show that the broad structure and position of the K-edge region can be modeled using density functional theory in combination with excited-state projector augmented-wave potentials. The density functional theory results are contrasted with a collisional-radiative model approach that incorporates ad-hoc density effects, which show incomplete agreement with the experimental observations, highlighting a need for improved density-dependent atomic modeling in warm dense plasmas.

AI.tldr: Experiments at the OMEGA laser facility compress and heat buried layer targets to warm dense matter (~20 eV, ~25 g/cm³), probed via x-ray absorption spectroscopy. Measured K-edge and bound-bound absorption features are compared against two modeling approaches: collisional-radiative models with ad-hoc density effects and DFT-based multi-ion models with excited-state PAW potentials. Neither fully reproduces the data, though DFT better captures the K-edge structure, highlighting the need for improved density-dependent atomic modeling.
AI.motivation: Warm dense matter is difficult to characterize experimentally and model predictively; controlled experiments with well-diagnosed platforms are needed to benchmark and advance theoretical models.
AI.method: Experiments at OMEGA compress/heated buried layer targets to warm dense conditions (~20 eV, 25 g/cm³), probed with x-ray absorption spectroscopy to extract K-edge and bound-bound absorption features for constraining temperature and charge state distribution. Measurements were compared with collisional-radiative models including ad-hoc density effects and a DFT-based multi-ion model using excited-state projector augmented-wave potentials.
AI.result: Neither modeling approach fully reproduces the observed data. The DFT-based model successfully captures the broad structure and position of the K-edge region, while the collisional-radiative model with ad-hoc density effects shows incomplete agreement with experiments.
AI.conclusion: DFT with excited-state PAW potentials performs better for K-edge spectral structure, but current density-dependent atomic modeling in warm dense plasmas is insufficient, highlighting the need for improved models.

title: Topological Effects on Bubbling in the Critical Dirichlet Problem on Hyperbolic Domains: $3\leq N \leq5$
summary:
Let \(Ω\Subset\mathbb H^N\), \(N\in\{3,4,5\}\), be a bounded connected \(C^2\) domain. We prove that the pure critical Dirichlet problem
  \[
  -Δ_{\mathbb H}u=u^{\frac{N+2}{N-2}}
  \quad\text{in }Ω,
  \qquad
  u=0
  \quad\text{on }\partialΩ
  \] admits a positive solution whenever \(H_d(Ω;\mathbb F_2)\neq0\) for some \(1\le d\le N-1\). This gives a hyperbolic Bahri-Coron theorem for \(3\le N\le5\) under \(C^2\) boundary regularity. Under conformal reduction, the hyperbolic geometry produces a positive potential and leads to dimension-dependent bubbling mechanisms. In dimension three, the required energy drop follows from the balance between diagonal corrections and pair interactions at fixed large multiplicity. In dimensions four and five, it is obtained at the matched scale through a normalized defect estimate and an all-pairs source-transfer bound. A unified Thom-barycenter construction converts these analytic estimates into the topological contradiction. Thus nontrivial domain topology forces existence despite critical loss of compactness and the additional geometric potential.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that the pure critical Dirichlet problem for the sub-Laplacian on the Heisenberg group admits a positive solution in bounded C² domains whenever the domain has nontrivial homology with F₂ coefficients, extending the Bahri-Coron theorem to the hyperbolic setting for dimensions 3≤N≤5.
AI.motivation: To establish a hyperbolic analogue of the classical Bahri-Coron theorem, showing that nontrivial domain topology forces the existence of positive solutions to a critical exponent Dirichlet problem, despite critical loss of compactness and the additional complications introduced by hyperbolic geometry and a positive potential term arising from conformal reduction.
AI.method: The proof combines conformal reduction (which produces a positive potential from hyperbolic geometry), dimension-dependent bubbling analysis with energy estimates—diagonal corrections versus pair interactions in N=3, and normalized defect estimates with all-pairs source-transfer bounds at matched scales in N=4,5—followed by a unified Thom-barycenter construction to derive the topological contradiction.
AI.result: A positive solution exists whenever H_d(Ω;F₂)≠0 for some 1≤d≤N−1, for N∈{3,4,5} with C² boundary regularity, giving a hyperbolic Bahri-Coron theorem under these conditions.
AI.conclusion: Nontrivial domain topology guarantees existence of positive critical solutions despite compactness loss and the geometric potential, with the proof achieved through carefully balanced dimension-dependent energy estimates and topological arguments.

title: An adaptive and conservative low-rank IMEX solver for the hybrid ion Vlasov-Fokker-Planck and fluid electron system
summary: We present a macroscopically conservative, rank-adaptive method for solving a hybrid Vlasov-Fokker-Planck (VFP) equation in which the ions are treated kinetically, and the electrons are treated as a fluid. Solving this system poses several coupled computational challenges: the curse of dimensionality, conservation of macroscopic quantities, stiffness arising from the multiscale nature of the model, and structure preservation. To address these challenges, we combine several established methods, each targeting a specific difficulty, into a unified framework for solving this nonlinear system. Specifically, we employ the recent Reduced Augmentation Implicit Low-rank (RAIL) method for rank adaptivity in velocity space to combat the curse of dimensionality, high-order implicit-explicit time stepping to handle the multiscale stiffness, and the Local Macroscopic Conservative (LoMaC) procedure for conservative truncation of the solution. The RAIL and LoMaC methods are extended from Cartesian to cylindrical coordinates. The resulting framework accommodates implicit rank-adaptive time integration while remaining conservative and leveraging structure-preserving discretizations. We verify the scheme on a suite of test problems and simulate a standing shock to demonstrate the importance of conserving the macroscopic quantities.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a macroscopically conservative, rank-adaptive method for solving a hybrid Vlasov-Fokker-Planck equation where ions are kinetic and electrons are fluid, combining RAIL rank-adaptivity, high-order implicit-explicit time stepping, and Local Macroscopic Conservative (LoMaC) truncation, with extensions to cylindrical coordinates.
AI.motivation: The hybrid Vlasov-Fokker-Planck system poses coupled computational challenges: the curse of dimensionality, conservation of macroscopic quantities, stiffness from multiscale nature, and structure preservation. These need to be addressed simultaneously in a unified framework.
AI.method: The framework combines several established methods: (1) Reduced Augmentation Implicit Low-rank (RAIL) for rank adaptivity in velocity space to combat curse of dimensionality, (2) high-order implicit-explicit time stepping for multiscale stiffness, and (3) Local Macroscopic Conservative (LoMaC) procedure for conservative truncation. RAIL and LoMaC are extended from Cartesian to cylindrical coordinates, enabling implicit rank-adaptive time integration while remaining conservative.
AI.result: The scheme is verified on a suite of test problems, and a standing shock simulation demonstrates the importance of conserving macroscopic quantities.
AI.conclusion: The proposed unified framework successfully addresses all coupled challenges of the hybrid VFP system—dimensionality, conservation, stiffness, and structure preservation—while being conservative and leveraging structure-preserving discretizations.

title: Resonant state expansion for acoustic resonators. Part I. Eigenvalue problem
summary: Resonant-state expansion (RSE) is a powerful modal framework for the perturbative analysis of open resonant systems, providing direct access to complex eigenfrequencies and eigenmodes. While RSE is well developed in electromagnetism, a comparably systematic formulation for acoustics remains less established. Here, we develop a general Green-function-based formalism for acoustic RSE and illustrate it for a class of two-dimensional acoustic resonators. Using the resonant states of an analytically solvable cylindrical reference system as a basis, we derive explicit perturbation matrix elements for uniform, radial, and sectoral variations of density and compressibility, representing homogeneous tuning, graded profiles, and symmetry-induced modal coupling. The resulting complex eigenfrequencies and eigenmodes are validated against exact analytical solutions and finite-element simulations, showing excellent quantitative agreement. The framework provides a systematic and physically transparent approach for analyzing perturbed open acoustic resonators and establishes a basis for resonant-state methods in acoustic metamaterials and non-Hermitian acoustics.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a general Green-function-based resonant-state expansion (RSE) formalism for acoustics, using analytically solvable cylindrical reference resonators as a basis to compute perturbed complex eigenfrequencies and eigenmodes for uniform, radial, and sectoral variations of density and compressibility, validated against exact solutions and finite-element simulations.
AI.motivation: While resonant-state expansion (RSE) is well-established for electromagnetic open resonant systems, a comparably systematic and general formulation for acoustics is lacking. The authors aim to fill this gap by developing a rigorous RSE framework suitable for acoustic resonators.
AI.method: The authors construct a Green-function-based RSE formalism for two-dimensional acoustic resonators. They use the resonant states of an analytically solvable cylindrical reference system as a basis, then derive explicit perturbation matrix elements for three types of perturbations: uniform (homogeneous tuning), radial (graded profiles), and sectoral (symmetry-induced modal coupling) variations in density and compressibility.
AI.result: The computed complex eigenfrequencies and eigenmodes show excellent quantitative agreement when validated against exact analytical solutions and finite-element simulations across all perturbation types considered.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a systematic and physically transparent approach for analyzing perturbed open acoustic resonators, establishing a foundation for applying resonant-state methods in acoustic metamaterials and non-Hermitian acoustics research.

title: Determining neutral fueling response to RMPs in MAST using a multi-reservoir particle balance model and EMC3 EIRENE
comment: 26 pages, 15 figures, submitted to Nuclear Fusion
summary: The application of certain configurations of resonant magnetic perturbations (RMPs) has been shown to cause a plasma pump-out in both L- and H-mode discharges at MAST. We discuss how this model was able to accurately reproduce the experimentally measured density reduction and ionization increase due to either a reduction in $τ_p$ or a reduction in particle fueling efficiency. Results from EMC3-EIRENE modeling indicate this change could be attributed to neutral particle fueling occurring in locations with now-opened field lines due to the chaotic edge-region from RMP applications.

title: Heat--Airy Transport of Differential Operators and Moving Boundaries
summary:
We study the transport of polynomial differential operators under the two-parameter commuting evolution \[ P_{t,s} =
\exp\left( \frac{t}{2}D^2-\frac{s}{3}D^3 \right), \qquad D=\frac{d}{dx}. \] Conjugation of the position operator gives \[ P_{t,s}xP_{t,s}^{-1} =
x+tD-sD^2, \] which leads to a recursive normal-ordering expansion and to a family of Heat--Airy polynomials arising as its derivative-free coefficients.
  Our main purpose is to study the interaction of this transport with moving absorbing boundaries. For functions satisfying \[ v_t=\frac12v_{xx}, \qquad v_s=-\frac13v_{xxx}, \qquad v(t,s,f(t,s))=0, \] the boundary condition generates a hierarchy of relations among the spatial jets of \(v\). Combined with the restrictions of transported differential equations and their spatial derivatives, these identities produce compatibility equations for \(f\).
  We prove a general restriction principle showing that, at every spatial-jet level, the compatibility equations of the classical Heat problem are obtained by restricting the corresponding Heat--Airy hierarchy to the slice \(s=0\). For second-order operators, this framework yields a finite characteristic system and nonlinear boundary equations, together with explicit solvable examples. For a third-order linear-potential operator, the additional Airy-flow identity permits a stronger sequential recovery: the first Heat--Airy compatibility equation determines \(f_s(t,0)\), and the next spatial-jet equation then reproduces the nonlinear compatibility condition obtained in the pure Heat theory from a \(4\times4\) characteristic determinant. Thus the additional commuting flow reorganizes the moving-boundary compatibility problem into a hierarchy while retaining the classical Heat theory as a distinguished restriction.

The authors develop a recursive normal-ordering expansion yielding Heat-Airy polynomials, and analyze moving absorbing boundaries by deriving compatibility equations for the boundary function f. They prove a restriction principle showing the classical Heat compatibility equations emerge as the s=0 slice of the Heat-Airy hierarchy, and demonstrate that for a third-order linear-potential operator, the additional Airy flow enables sequential recovery of compatibility conditions, reorganizing the moving-boundary problem into a hierarchy.
AI.motivation: To understand how commuting flows (heat and Airy) interact with moving absorbing boundaries, and to find a unified framework that generalizes the classical heat problem's moving-boundary compatibility equations into a hierarchy, while preserving the classical theory as a distinguished restriction.
AI.method: The authors conjugate the position operator under the two-parameter evolution P_{t,s} = exp(t/2 D² - s/3 D³), obtaining x + tD - sD², which yields a recursive normal-ordering expansion and Heat-Airy polynomials. They then study moving absorbing boundaries v(t,s,f(t,s))=0, deriving jet-level relations, and combine these with restricted transported differential equations to produce compatibility equations for f. A general restriction principle is proved showing the s=0 slice recovers the classical Heat problem compatibility equations.

For second-order operators, a finite characteristic system and nonlinear boundary equations are derived with explicit solvable examples. title: Evo-GTransNet for Parabolic PDEs: A Fixed-Feature Galerkin Method of Lines with Quadrature-Mass Orthonormalization
summary: In this paper, we develop an evolutionary generalized transferable neural network (Evo-GTransNet) solver for parabolic partial differential equations, formulated as a retained-space fixed-feature Galerkin method of lines. A GTransNet provides the prescribed spatial dictionary, while only the retained output coefficients evolve, thereby avoiding nonlinear training during time integration. To address severe mass-matrix ill-conditioning, we apply a quadrature-weighted truncated singular value decomposition (SVD) to select the numerically resolved trial space, followed by a separate rescaling that makes its basis orthonormal with respect to the assembly-quadrature mass inner product. Rank truncation modifies the approximation space, whereas the subsequent orthonormalization changes only its coordinate representation and preserves the retained discrete functions in exact arithmetic. The resulting semidiscrete coefficient system has an identity mass matrix, and we establish a semidiscrete energy law for symmetric linear parabolic problems. With the implicit midpoint scheme for time discretization, we further prove the contractivity of the method and derive a conditional fully discrete error estimate in which the error is controlled by the retained-space approximation error and the consistency defects. Numerical experiments demonstrate second-order temporal convergence using repeated feature samples together with separate assembly and validation quadratures, and quantify the accuracy of the retained space in the presence of severe raw-mass ill-conditioning. For the high-frequency and multiscale benchmark problems considered here, GTransNet achieves the smallest mean validation errors among the tested fixed-feature dictionaries at the same nominal output dimension.

AI.tldr: The paper develops Evo-GTransNet, an evolutionary generalized transferable neural network solver for parabolic PDEs, formulated as a retained-space fixed-feature Galerkin method of lines. It uses a quadrature-weighted truncated SVD to handle severe mass-matrix ill-conditioning, followed by orthonormalization. The method proves semidiscrete energy laws, contractivity with implicit midpoint scheme, and conditional fully discrete error estimates, with numerical experiments demonstrating second-order temporal convergence.
AI.motivation: To develop a neural network-based solver for parabolic PDEs that avoids nonlinear training during time integration, while addressing the severe mass-matrix ill-conditioning that arises in such fixed-feature Galerkin formulations.
AI.method: A GTransNet provides a prescribed spatial dictionary with only retained output coefficients evolving. A quadrature-weighted truncated SVD selects the numerically resolved trial space, followed by rescaling for orthonormality with respect to the assembly-quadrature mass inner product. The resulting system has an identity mass matrix, combined with implicit midpoint time discretization.
AI.result: Numerical experiments show second-order temporal convergence with repeated feature samples and separate assembly/validation quadratures. GTransNet achieves the smallest mean validation errors among tested fixed-feature dictionaries at the same nominal output dimension for high-frequency and multiscale benchmark problems.
AI.conclusion: The method establishes semidiscrete energy laws for symmetric linear parabolic problems, proves contractivity with implicit midpoint scheme, and derives a conditional fully discrete error estimate controlled by retained-space approximation error and consistency defects.

title: Resonant state expansion for acoustic resonators. Part II. Scattering problem
summary: We develop a resonant-state expansion formulation for acoustic scattering by individual resonators. The scattered pressure and particle-velocity fields are expanded over the resonant states of the system, with excitation amplitudes determined by overlap integrals between the incident field and the resonant states over the resonator volume. Using the acoustic energy flux, we derive expressions for the extinction, scattering, and absorption cross-sections and show that the extinction spectrum can be resolved into contributions from individual resonant states. The formulation is first validated for a homogeneous two-dimensional cylinder, where it reproduces the analytical Mie-theory solution. We then consider a sectorally perturbed cylinder with coupled azimuthal modes and demonstrate agreement with finite-element simulations. Finally, we combine the eigenvalue and scattering formulations for a material-programmed hard-wall annular metaatom and reproduce its scattering spectra and near fields. The developed framework provides a physically transparent modal approach to acoustic scattering by open resonators with reduced symmetry and spatially structured material parameters.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a resonant-state expansion (RSE) formulation for acoustic scattering by individual resonators, where scattered fields are expanded over resonant states with amplitudes determined by overlap integrals with the incident field. The framework derives extinction, scattering, and absorption cross-sections from acoustic energy flux, is validated against Mie theory and finite-element simulations, and offers a physically transparent modal approach for open resonators with reduced symmetry and structured materials.
AI.motivation: To provide a physically transparent modal framework for understanding acoustic scattering by open resonators, particularly those with reduced symmetry (e.g., sectorally perturbed cylinders) and spatially structured material parameters (e.g., material-programmed metaatoms), where traditional approaches may lack interpretability or computational efficiency.
AI.method: The authors formulate a resonant-state expansion (RSE) for acoustic scattering, expressing scattered pressure and particle-velocity fields as superpositions of system resonant states. Excitation amplitudes are computed via overlap integrals between the incident field and resonant states over the resonator volume. Cross-sections (extinction, scattering, absorption) are derived using acoustic energy flux, with the extinction spectrum decomposed into individual resonant-state contributions. The method is applied to a homogeneous cylinder, a sectorally perturbed cylinder with coupled azimuthal modes, and a material-programmed hard-wall annular metaatom.
AI.result: The formulation reproduces the analytical Mie-theory solution for a homogeneous 2D cylinder, agrees with finite-element simulations for a sectorally perturbed cylinder with coupled azimuthal modes, and successfully reproduces scattering spectra and near fields of a material-programmed hard-wall annular metaatom.
AI.conclusion: The RSE framework provides a physically interpretable modal approach to acoustic scattering by open resonators, extending applicability to systems with reduced symmetry and spatially structured material parameters while enabling decomposition of extinction spectra into individual resonant-state contributions.

title: Characterizing the temporal evolution of Biermann-battery-driven magnetic reconnection in laser-ablated plasmas
comment: Accepted for publication in Physical Review E. The paper is 12 pages long with 10 figures
summary: This paper presents an experimental investigation of magnetic reconnection between two laser-produced expanding plasmas, focusing on the quantitative evaluation of the reconnection rate and energy conversion under varying initial conditions. By changing the separation distance between the drive laser focal spots (1 mm and 2 mm), we systematically controlled the inflow parameters. The reconnection region was probed using a two-directional laser Thomson scattering (LTS) system, which simultaneously measured the local plasma parameters parallel to the outflows and along the current sheet. Based on our established method incorporating macroscopic energy and mass conservation laws to derive the upstream magnetic field directly from LTS spectra, we characterized the temporal evolution of the current sheet and the reconnection rate. The larger spot separation allows the plasma bubbles to expand for a substantially longer time before the formation of a reconnection current sheet, resulting in different upstream conditions. Nevertheless, both configurations yielded comparable upstream magnetic fields and reconnection rates. These results suggest that the reconnection rate is relatively insensitive to the global inflow conditions and is primarily controlled by the local physics of the reconnection layer once a current sheet is formed.

Using two-directional laser Thomson scattering to measure plasma parameters, they found that despite different upstream conditions from different expansion times, both configurations yielded comparable upstream magnetic fields and reconnection rates, suggesting reconnection rate is governed by local layer physics rather than global inflow conditions.
AI.motivation: To quantitatively evaluate the reconnection rate and energy conversion under varying initial conditions in laser-produced plasma magnetic reconnection experiments, and to determine whether global inflow conditions or local physics control the reconnection rate.
AI.method: Experiments with two separation distances (1mm and 2mm) between laser focal spots to control inflow parameters. A two-directional laser Thomson scattering (LTS) system simultaneously measured local plasma parameters parallel to outflows and along the current sheet. Magnetic field was derived from LTS spectra using macroscopic energy and mass conservation laws to characterize current sheet evolution and reconnection rates.

title: Solutions to a One-Dimensional Combustion-Type Free Boundary Problem via Maximal Regularity
summary: We study a one-dimensional free boundary problem arising in combustion theory, where the motion of the interface is governed by a prescribed Neumann boundary flux and a zero Dirichlet boundary condition. We treat both the half-line case and the bounded interval case. For both settings, we employ maximal $L^p$-$L^q$ regularity as our main analytical tool. In the half-line case, the solutions need not decay at infinity, even though the spatial derivatives belong to $L^q(\mathbb{R}_+)$. To handle the evolution law of the free boundary, we introduce a derivative formulation that avoids second-order boundary traces. By combining maximal $L^p$-$L^q$ regularity and Schauder estimates, we establish the local-in-time existence, uniqueness, and regularity of solutions, as well as the evolution law of the free boundary.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes a one-dimensional free boundary problem from combustion theory with prescribed Neumann flux and zero Dirichlet conditions, using maximal Lp-Lq regularity to establish local-in-time existence, uniqueness, and regularity on both half-line and bounded interval domains.
AI.motivation: To solve a one-dimensional free boundary problem in combustion theory where the interface motion is governed by Neumann and Dirichlet boundary conditions, which requires new analytical tools due to the non-decay of solutions at infinity.
AI.method: Employs maximal Lp-Lq regularity combined with Schauder estimates. Introduces a derivative formulation to avoid second-order boundary traces, handling both half-line and bounded interval cases.
AI.result: Establishes local-in-time existence, uniqueness, and regularity of solutions, along with the explicit evolution law of the free boundary.
AI.conclusion: The combination of maximal Lp-Lq regularity and Schauder estimates provides an effective framework for solving this free boundary problem, even when solutions do not decay at infinity.

title: Learning Deterministic and Stochastic Forced Hamiltonian Systems
summary: We develop a geometric framework for learning deterministic and stochastic forced Hamiltonian systems with neural networks. Motivated by the Lagrange-d'Alembert principle and the theory of variational integrators, we introduce the notion of a Lagrange-d'Alembert map and establish a $C^r$ convergence theorem for first-order one-step methods. Building on these results, we propose Generalized Forced Hamiltonian Neural Networks (GFHNNs), a class of structure-preserving neural networks obtained by concatenating Lagrange-d'Alembert-Euler maps, and prove a universal approximation theorem for this architecture. We further extend the framework to parameter-dependent systems, leading to Parametric Generalized Forced Hamiltonian Neural Networks (PGFHNNs). By interpreting the multiple Stratonovich integrals appearing in the Stratonovich-Taylor expansion as parameters, the same framework can be applied to stochastic forced Hamiltonian systems whenever information about the underlying Wiener process is available. Our numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed geometric architectures provide significantly improved long-time stability and accuracy compared to non-geometric residual neural networks, while requiring substantially less training data to achieve a comparable level of performance.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a geometric framework for learning forced Hamiltonian systems (deterministic and stochastic) using neural networks, via a novel "Lagrange-d'Alembert map" and Generalized Forced Hamiltonian Neural Networks (GFHNNs) that preserve the underlying geometric structure.
AI.motivation: Standard neural networks for modeling dynamical systems lack structural guarantees (e.g., symplecticity, energy preservation), leading to poor long-time stability and requiring large amounts of training data. The authors aim to develop structure-preserving neural architectures grounded in geometric mechanics.
AI.method: The authors introduce a Lagrange-d'Alembert map (motivated by the Lagrange-d'Alembert principle and variational integrators), prove a C^r convergence theorem for first-order one-step methods, and construct GFHNNs by concatenating Lagrange-d'Alembert-Euler maps (with a universal approximation theorem). They extend this to Parametric GFHNNs (PGFHNNs) for parameter-dependent systems, and further apply the framework to stochastic forced Hamiltonian systems by treating multiple Stratonovich integrals as parameters.
AI.result: Numerical experiments show that the proposed geometric architectures (GFHNNs/PGFHNNs) achieve significantly improved long-time stability and accuracy compared to non-geometric residual neural networks, while requiring substantially less training data for comparable performance.
AI.conclusion: Geometric structure-preserving neural architectures based on the Lagrange-d'Alembert framework offer a principled and effective approach for learning forced Hamiltonian systems, outperforming generic neural networks in both accuracy and data efficiency.

title: Dynamic Ensembles of Phosphine-Stabilized Gold Nanoclusters
summary: Atomically precise phosphine-stabilized gold nanoclusters are commonly characterized by single-crystal X-ray diffraction, yet the extent to which these static structures represent finite-temperature behavior remains unclear. To explore the free-energy landscapes, equilibrium populations, and isomerization kinetics of these nanoclusters in the gas phase, we establish a general framework that combines molecular dynamics simulations based on a machine-learned interatomic potential with Markov state models (MSMs). Analysis of the MSMs indicates that experimentally reported crystal structures frequently correspond to minor metastable states or transient configurations rather than the dominant finite-temperature structures. Increasing ligand coverage systematically alters both the thermodynamics and kinetics of structural rearrangements, driving the transition from planar to three-dimensional gold cores while accelerating isomerization dynamics. Moreover, catalytically accessible geometries are often only minor members of the equilibrium ensemble, highlighting a trade-off between structural stability and surface accessibility. These results emphasize that ligand-protected nanoclusters need to be viewed as dynamic ensembles and their finite-temperature behavior cannot be fully captured by their corresponding crystallographic structures alone.

The findings reveal that experimentally reported crystal structures often correspond to minor metastable or transient states rather than dominant finite-temperature structures, with ligand coverage systematically altering both thermodynamics and kinetics.

AI.method: A general framework combining molecular dynamics simulations based on a machine-learned interatomic potential with Markov state models (MSMs) to explore free-energy landscapes, equilibrium populations, and isomerization kinetics of gold nanoclusters in the gas phase.
AI.result: Experimentally reported crystal structures frequently correspond to minor metastable states or transient configurations rather than dominant finite-temperature structures. Increasing ligand coverage systematically alters thermodynamics and kinetics, driving transitions from planar to three-dimensional gold cores while accelerating isomerization dynamics. title: Collisionless Resonances Set the Size of a Weyl Exceptional Ring
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures; Supplemental Material appended. Data and code are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22020911
summary: Eliminating continuum degrees of freedom converts conservative dynamics into a dispersive, non-Hermitian response whose topology need not represent the causally selected kinetic dynamics. In collisionless magnetized plasma, retarded Landau and cyclotron resonances damp two Weyl modes differently and replace a cold Weyl point by an exceptional ring. Axial roots and root-normalized polarization mixing predict its off-axis radius, $R_{\rm EP}^{\rm pred}=|ΔΓ|/(2|v_{\rm mix}|)$, before any double root is computed. Across five nonrelativistic scans spanning a 310-fold range of differential damping, $R_{\rm EP}^{\rm pred}$ agrees with the nonlinear double-root radius $R_{\rm EP}^{\rm full}$ within $0.12\%$. The selected retarded kinetic-response bundle is a continuous graph over the electric root line bundle and has the same first Chern class under stated conditions. The cold interface mode continues to a localized Keldysh pole with one oriented crossing in the tested line-gap window, consistent with the inherited charge.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that eliminating continuum degrees of freedom in collisionless magnetized plasma transforms conservative dynamics into dispersive, non-Hermitian response, where retarded Landau/cyclotron resonances damp two Weyl modes differently and replace a cold Weyl point with an exceptional ring. The authors derive a root-normalized polarization mixing prediction for the exceptional ring radius that matches full nonlinear double-root calculations within 0.12% across five scans spanning a 310-fold range of differential damping.
AI.motivation: To understand how continuum degrees of freedom, when eliminated, alter the topology of kinetic plasma dynamics—specifically whether the non-Hermitian response topology faithfully represents the causally selected kinetic dynamics.
AI.method: The authors analyze retarded kinetic response in collisionless magnetized plasma, computing exceptional ring radii via two routes: (1) a predictive formula using axial roots and root-normalized polarization mixing, R_EP^pred = |ΔΓ|/(2|v_mix|), and (2) full nonlinear double-root calculations. They compare these across five nonrelativistic parameter scans and examine the resulting line bundle topology and first Chern class, plus the continuation of cold interface modes to localized Keldysh poles.

The retarded kinetic-response bundle is a continuous graph over the electric root line bundle with the same first Chern class under stated conditions, and the cold interface mode continues to a localized Keldysh pole with one oriented crossing in the tested line-gap window.
AI.conclusion: The topology of the causally selected (retarded) kinetic response is determined by the electric root line bundle and does not necessarily match that of the naive conservative expectation. A simple analytic prediction accurately captures the exceptional ring radius, confirming that non-Hermitian response topology can be predicted before full spectral computation, and the inherited interface-mode charge is preserved in the kinetic extension.

title: Global Well-Posedness near Rayleigh-Jeans Equilibria for the Cubic NLS Wave Kinetic Equation
summary: We study the dynamics of the kinetic wave equation associated to the three dimensional Schrödinger equation close to Rayleigh-Jeans equilibria. We first prove that the linearised operator generates a semigroup of contractions in $L^2((0,\infty);\sqrt ω\ddω)$. Considering the family of nonsingular Rayleigh-Jeans spectra, we prove that the linearised operator possesses a spectral gap, despite the non-compactness of the integral collisional operator, and thus obtain an exponential relaxation for the linear semigroup. We then prove bilinear and trilinear estimates in the relevant norm for the nonlinear terms and deduce global well-posedness and exponential relaxation for sufficiently small relative perturbations of Rayleigh-Jeans equilibria. To our knowledge, this is the first global strong well-posedness and asymptotic stability result near a nonzero thermodynamic equilibrium for the full spatially homogeneous four-wave kinetic equation associated with the cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the kinetic wave equation for the 3D cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation near Rayleigh-Jeans equilibria, proving the linearized operator generates a contraction semigroup, establishing a spectral gap (despite non-compactness), and deriving bilinear/trilinear estimates leading to global well-posedness and exponential relaxation for small perturbations.
AI.motivation: To establish the first global strong well-posedness and asymptotic stability result near nonzero thermodynamic equilibrium for the full spatially homogeneous four-wave kinetic equation associated with the cubic NLS equation.
AI.method: The authors (1) prove the linearized operator around Rayleigh-Jeans equilibria generates a contraction semigroup in a weighted L² space, (2) show the linearized operator possesses a spectral gap for nonsingular Rayleigh-Jeans spectra despite the non-compactness of the integral collisional operator, yielding exponential relaxation, and (3) prove bilinear and trilinear estimates for nonlinear terms to close the argument.
AI.result: Exponential relaxation for the linear semigroup, global well-posedness, and exponential relaxation for sufficiently small relative perturbations of Rayleigh-Jeans equilibria.
AI.conclusion: This is the first global strong well-posedness and asymptotic stability result near a nonzero thermodynamic equilibrium for the full spatially homogeneous four-wave kinetic equation associated with the cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation.

title: Exact hierarchical algorithms for accelerating particle--mesh coupling in sparse-grid particle-in-cell methods
summary: In this paper, we propose two hierarchical algorithms for charge deposition and electric-field interpolation that apply to both the sparse-grid combination technique (SGCT-PIC) and hierarchical sparse-grid (HSG-PIC) particle-in-cell methods. The two algorithms are inspired by the fast multipole method (FMM) and exploit clusters of particles associated with a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of particle-populated boxes to reduce the number of particle--mesh interactions. The particle--mesh interactions are governed by piecewise-polynomial kernels, so that the associated multipole expansions are exact, requiring neither truncation nor approximation, and are valid in both near- and far-field regions, thereby eliminating the need for multipole-to-local translations. The arithmetic complexity of the charge deposition and field interpolation steps is reduced from $Ø(p^d n^{d-1}N)$ to $Ø(p^d(N+M))$, where $M=2^{dn}$ denotes the number of full-grid mesh nodes and is typically no larger than the particle population in the considered regime, $M\lesssim N$. Numerical experiments in two-dimensional configurations demonstrate charge-deposition speedups of $8.2\times$--$66.9\times$ for SGCT-PIC and $3.1\times$--$18.8\times$ for HSG-PIC, and field-interpolation speedups of $4.1\times$--$62.6\times$ and $4.2\times$--$13.7\times$, respectively, depending on the particle-per-cell ratio, while preserving the exact particle--mesh interactions. The speedups increase with the particle-per-cell ratio, reflecting the reduced dependence of the hierarchical algorithms on the number of particles and their increasing advantage for large particle populations.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes two hierarchical algorithms for charge deposition and field interpolation in sparse-grid and hierarchical sparse-grid particle-in-cell methods, inspired by the fast multipole method, that reduce arithmetic complexity from O(p^d n^{d-1}N) to O(p^d(N+M)) while preserving exact particle-mesh interactions. Numerical experiments show speedups of up to 66.9x for charge deposition and up to 62.6x for field interpolation in 2D configurations.
AI.motivation: The standard particle-mesh interactions in sparse-grid and hierarchical sparse-grid particle-in-cell methods are computationally expensive, scaling with O(p^d n^{d-1}N), which becomes prohibitive for large particle populations. The authors aim to reduce this computational burden by exploiting the hierarchical structure of particle clusters, inspired by the fast multipole method.

Since particle-mesh interactions use piecewise-polynomial kernels, the multipole expansions are exact (no truncation or approximation) and valid in both near- and far-field regions, eliminating the need for multipole-to-local translations. The complexity is reduced from O(p^d n^{d-1}N) to O(p^d(N+M)), where M is the number of full-grid mesh nodes.
AI.result: In 2D numerical experiments, the algorithms achieve charge-deposition speedups of 8.2x-66.9x for SGCT-PIC and 3.1x-18.8x for HSG-PIC, and field-interpolation speedups of 4.1x-62.6x and 4.2x-13.7x respectively, while preserving exact particle-mesh interactions. Speedups increase with the particle-per-cell ratio.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical algorithms significantly accelerate the particle-mesh interaction steps in sparse-grid PIC methods, with increasing advantage for large particle populations. The exactness of the piecewise-polynomial multipole expansions ensures the physical accuracy is maintained, and the complexity reduction makes these methods more scalable for large-scale simulations.

title: Kerr Quasinormal Modes without Variable Separation: A Two-Dimensional Hyperboloidal Teukolsky Solver with Physics-Informed Neural Networks
summary: We use physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) to solve the gravitational quasinormal-mode (QNM) eigenvalue problem for Kerr spacetime directly in the two-dimensional hyperboloidal formulation of the Teukolsky equation. This formulation does not require separation of variables and thus retains the coupled radial--angular structure. Such a scheme provides a prototype for calculating the QNMs of beyond-Kerr black holes for which the perturbation equations are non-separable. Sequences with increasing angular momentum are constructed, reaching close to the extremal limit. We focus on the fundamental modes $(\ell,m,n)=(2,0,0)$, $(2,1,0)$, $(2,2,0)$, $(3,3,0)$ and $(4,4,0)$, together with the first overtone $(2,2,1)$. Independent benchmark evaluation shows that every reported real and imaginary frequency component remains below $0.5\%$ error, with a median deviation of $0.1\%$. This accuracy is maintained in the near-extremal regime, where the damping rate becomes small and the modes are longest-lived. The results establish a non-spectral numerical route to multidimensional black-hole perturbation eigenproblems which does not match the substantially higher precision of dedicated Kerr solvers but offers greater flexibility and requires less analytical pre-processing. Non-separable rotating backgrounds and coupled systems, such as gravitational--electromagnetic Kerr--Newman perturbations, are natural extensions of the same construction.

AI.tldr: The paper uses physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) to solve the gravitational quasinormal-mode eigenvalue problem for Kerr spacetime in a two-dimensional hyperboloidal formulation of the Teukolsky equation without variable separation. Results achieve <0.5% error for all tested modes including near-extremal cases, establishing a flexible non-spectral numerical approach for multidimensional black-hole perturbation problems.
AI.motivation: Traditional Kerr QNM solvers rely on separation of variables (radial and angular), which fails for beyond-Kerr black holes where perturbation equations are non-separable. A numerical approach that retains the coupled radial-angular structure is needed as a prototype for computing QNMs of non-separable black hole spacetimes.
AI.method: Use physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) to directly solve the QNM eigenvalue problem in the two-dimensional hyperboloidal formulation of the Teukolsky equation for Kerr spacetime, avoiding variable separation and preserving the coupled radial-angular structure. Construct sequences with increasing angular momentum approaching the extremal limit, targeting fundamental modes and one overtone.
AI.result: All reported real and imaginary frequency components have below 0.5% error with a median deviation of 0.1%, including in the near-extremal regime where damping rates are small and modes are longest-lived. Accuracy is maintained while offering a more flexible approach than dedicated Kerr solvers, though it does not match their substantially higher precision.
AI.conclusion: The PINN approach establishes a viable non-spectral numerical route to multidimensional black-hole perturbation eigenproblems. It requires less analytical pre-processing and offers greater flexibility, making non-separable rotating backgrounds and coupled systems like Kerr-Newman gravitational-electromagnetic perturbations natural extensions.

title: Revisiting the Growth Rate of the Relativistic Tearing Instability: The Role of the Non-ideal MHD Structure
summary: Magnetic reconnection in magnetically dominated pair plasmas is a key process in high-energy astrophysical systems. We revisit the relativistic tearing instability in a Harris current sheet and derive an improved analytical expression for its linear growth rate and the most unstable wavenumber. The key modification is the treatment of the vector potential perturbation in the non-ideal magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) region. Instead of the conventional constant-A approximation, we use an extrapolated-A approximation, in which the ideal-MHD solution is linearly extrapolated into the non-ideal region. Comparison with two-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations shows that the revised theory improves the prediction of the most unstable wavenumber. The improvement is most pronounced at low particle drift velocities, where the particle gyroradius is smaller than the current-sheet thickness and the fastest-growing mode shifts to longer wavelength. The resulting analytical expressions provide an updated benchmark for magnetically dominated reconnection and its applications to high-energy astrophysical plasmas, including gamma-ray bursts and fast radio bursts.

AI.tldr: The authors revisit the relativistic tearing instability in Harris current sheets and derive an improved analytical expression for the linear growth rate and most unstable wavenumber by using an extrapolated-A approximation instead of the conventional constant-A approximation for the vector potential perturbation in the non-ideal MHD region. The revised theory, validated against 2D particle-in-cell simulations, improves predictions of the most unstable wavenumber, especially at low particle drift velocities where the fastest-growing mode shifts to longer wavelengths.
AI.motivation: Magnetic reconnection in magnetically dominated pair plasmas is a critical process in high-energy astrophysical systems, yet existing analytical treatments of the relativistic tearing instability have limitations. The conventional constant-A approximation fails to accurately predict the most unstable wavenumber, motivating the need for an improved analytical framework.
AI.method: The authors derive an improved analytical expression for the linear growth rate and most unstable wavenumber of the relativistic tearing instability. Instead of the constant-A approximation, they employ an extrapolated-A approximation, where the ideal-MHD solution is linearly extrapolated into the non-ideal region. They validate the revised theory against 2D particle-in-cell simulations.
AI.result: The revised theory improves the prediction of the most unstable wavenumber compared to the conventional approach. The improvement is most significant at low particle drift velocities, where the particle gyroradius is smaller than the current-sheet thickness and the fastest-growing mode shifts to longer wavelengths.
AI.conclusion: The resulting analytical expressions provide an updated benchmark for magnetically dominated reconnection, with applications to high-energy astrophysical plasmas including gamma-ray bursts and fast radio bursts.

title: Higher order logarithms of Bessel operators and an extension problem
summary: We consider the Bessel operator defined by \[ B_λ=-\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+\frac{λ^2-1/4}{x^2}, \] on $(0,\infty)$, with $λ>-1$. We study the fractional power $B_λ^s$, $s\in (-1,1)$, $s\neq 0$, and the logarithm $\log^kB_λ$, $k\in \mathbb N$, of $B_λ$. We obtain pointwise representations of these operators and asymptotic Taylor expansions of the operators $B_λ^s$ in terms of logarithmic operators $\log^kB_λ$. We also obtain $\log B_λ$ as the solution of an extension problem.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the Bessel operator B_λ on (0,∞), investigating its fractional powers B_λ^s and logarithmic powers log^k B_λ, deriving pointwise representations, asymptotic Taylor expansions of B_λ^s in terms of logarithmic operators, and solving an extension problem for log B_λ.
AI.motivation: To develop a deeper understanding of the Bessel operator's functional calculus, particularly its fractional and logarithmic powers, which are important in harmonic analysis and partial differential equations.
AI.method: The authors obtain pointwise integral representations for the fractional powers B_λ^s and logarithmic operators log^k B_λ, derive asymptotic Taylor expansions relating these operators, and formulate log B_λ as the solution of a suitable extension problem.
AI.result: Pointwise representations of B_λ^s and log^k B_λ are obtained, along with asymptotic Taylor expansions of B_λ^s in terms of logarithmic operators, and a characterization of log B_λ via an extension problem.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a complete functional calculus framework for the Bessel operator, connecting fractional powers, logarithmic operators, and extension problems, which has implications for related PDEs and interpolation theory.

title: Optimal Sobolev Approximation by Deterministic and Random Shallow Sigmoidal Networks
